This is awesome Kiran! Do you have any particular use cases in mind for where lean.py should be applied? Will it be useful for verification of Python programs? Or is it more for library development, similarly to how Python libraries like Numpy call into C++ for performance reasons?

I think the sympy and knuckle tactics are very cool ideas. But it would of course be better if sympy.simplify returned an actual proof certificate so you don't have to invoke oracle axioms every time you use them. I could see Python-based tactics being a very powerful tool in the future if that could be sorted out.

Hi Jack! Thanks. With respect to your questions:

Do you have any particular use cases in mind for where lean.py should be applied?

So to clarify, I see this as more foundational infrastructure. It builds on two observations, the first being that the python ecosystem is very rich and would be useful to have access to in lean, and second being that with projects such as Loom and Velvet, Lean is quickly becoming quite a useful general library for domain specific verifiers, or as a symbolic reasoning engine.

Lean.py serves as what I believe to be the necessary component to enable both of these use cases. It is at its core just a general shim between lean and python, allowing manipulating runtime objects in one language in another. I wouldn't want to constrain the applications of such a shim by claiming that it's aimed at any particular domain.

Will it be useful for verification of Python programs? Or is it more for library development, similarly to how Python libraries like Numpy call into C++ for performance reasons?

These, sure are certainly possible ways in which you could use this kind of shim. Python has a rather rich infrastructure for runtime introspection and metaprogramming, and you could use this shim to translate python objects to lean and construct corresponding verification conditions. Similarly, it could also be used to call python libraries in Lean. It's a general shim, allowing bridging runtime objects from one ecosystem to the other. I would hope that the applications are quite plentiful.

I think the sympy and knuckle tactics are very cool ideas. But it would of course be better if sympy.simplify returned an actual proof certificate so you don't have to invoke oracle axioms every time you use them. I could see Python-based tactics being a very powerful tool in the future if that could be sorted out.

Thanks! I hope I didn't give the impression that these < 100 line proof of concept snippets were intended to be tactics to be applied in anger in real lean projects. These are merely demos, but yes, if one were interested, one could certainly flesh them out to do some kind of proof reconstruction. You might be interested in the very rich literature of SMT proof term reconstruction, which provides some insights on how the outputs of these kinds of efficient solvers can then be translated back into proof terms. Of course, as a simple demo, I wanted to keep this small and concise, and not clutter the example code with a more fleshed out reconstruction logic which would have been orthogonal to the pedagogical goals of the code itself.

That makes sense. I suppose I was curious whether there was a specific project that you are working on that motivated the creation of lean.py. Do you have plans to build on top of it? Or are you waiting to see what the community does with it?
Very cool project! Do you think a similar technique could be used to make a javascript bridge?

@Jack McCarthy ah, I see! In that case, I guess two answers:

my real (non-work) reason? I like using Lean for building DSLs and I wanted to use it to build a DSL for games in godot. I tried setting up FFI to bind to it, but that ended up being a bigger task than anticipated. Targeting python as a glue between the two (there is a godot python binding) seemed more manageable.

My work answer would be, we have a library https://github.com/BasisResearch/effectful which has a lightweight embedding of (non-control) algebraic effects in python, which turns out to be quite useful for embedding DSLs in Python.

Using effectful, I added a new example to lean.py which implements a python verification layer which generates VCs in Lean and attempts to verify these python functions by using Omega and grind:

def positive_increment(x: Annotated[int, Gt(0)]):
    y = x + 3
    assert_refined(y, Gt(3))      # x > 0 → x + 3 > 3   ✓
    z = x + 10
    assert_refined(z, Gt(10))     # x > 0 → x + 10 > 10  ✓
assert verify(positive_increment)

def bounded_sum(x: Annotated[int, Gt(0)], y: Annotated[int, Gt(0)]):
    s = x + y
    assert_refined(s, Gt(1))      # x > 0 ∧ y > 0 → x + y > 1   ✓
    assert_refined(s, Ge(2))      # x > 0 ∧ y > 0 → x + y >= 2  ✓
assert verify(bounded_sum)


def failing(x: Annotated[int, Gt(0)]):
    y = x + 1
    assert_refined(y, Gt(10))     # x > 0 → x + 1 > 10  ✗
assert not verify(failing)

https://github.com/BasisResearch/lean.py/blob/main/examples/06_effectful_verifier/python/main.py

Very cool project! Do you think a similar technique could be used to make a javascript bridge?

@nrs I think so. I don't know if Javascript has a standardised ffi, so you might need to pick one of the JS interpreters? I think the nice thing about python is that I can just target Cpython and provide broad support to most people using Python

@Kiran That's a great reason. I love Godot. Open source game engines are epic. Btw I just played "Kiran's Day Off", it takes me back to when I was a little kid playing Cookie Clickers with my brother. I do look forward to your future games.

Regarding effectful, I did not know much about effect systems prior to today, so this was good reading material. I am still trying to understand the "Example 3: Associative Semigroups" in the effectful documentation (the associative_add and associative_commutative_add functions bamboozle me with their _ {} ()). Your 06_effectful_verifier is clearer in terms of what all the handlers are doing. The implementation of refine.py and exprBuilder.py are simple, but I would love to see how far we could build them out. Could turn into powerful framework for formal verification in Python. Although the logic for closing goals would of course need to be more sophisticated than intros; simp [Int.ofNat] at *; omega.

On a side note: the connection to the Pyro/ChiRho ecosystem. Do you do much probabilistic programming? I've been learning Pyro myself, and would love to get your insight on the topic, especially as it relates to Lean/formalization.

Here's another example of a little demo I threw today using lean.py!

This is a little string-diagram-based proof visualizer I threw together today. I've been reading Fong and Spivak's applied category theory, and ch2 goes into how monoidal pre-orders can be represented using string diagrams and then goes through a number of domains.

To play around with string diagrams and help understanding, I built a little tool that allows me to visualize and build these string diagrams. Under the hood, to avoid re-implementing my own symbolic-reasoning engine, I just use lean.py to setup a lean goal and then apply tactics to update the goal state and update the UI to match.

So cool! I wonder how this compares to https://github.com/leanprover/nerodia ? Seems like they're quite different but the use case is somewhat adjacent?

Oh! I was totally unaware of nerodia! That's a cool project! I think we have similar/some overlaps in usecases. My primary motivation was after getting tired of writing C-ffi's in Lean and instead wanting a single common interface for accessing C libraries from Lean (for which python serves as a nice intermediate glue). Nerodia seems to be primarily at exposing Lean modules to Python - so it seems like it might lack the ability for callbacks or closures etc.

Lean.py supports bidirectional interaction between lean and python, exploiting both langauges' dynamic/extensible nature, so you could call Python from lean etc.

I'm curious what the usecase for nerodia is, I can't see many places where people would want to use Lean code directly from Python, the other direction seems more helpful for me.
